Q: Unable to allocate TiB for an array with shape data type uint8 A:

If you expect most of the entries in this array to be 0, you might want to use a sparse array instead.

Sparse arrays are data structures which only store non-zero entries.

There are multiple underlying representations for sparse arrays available in scipy.sparse, which will have different performance trade offs.

https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/sparse.html

Q: Bulk-load large graphs into FalkorDB A:

The bulk-loader is the most efficient way to load such bulk see: https://docs.falkordb.com/integration/bulk-loader.html

Or you can use the CSV LOAD command which can give you more flexibility see: https://docs.falkordb.com/cypher/load-csv.html

Q: BigQuery - NULL values A:

You could also handle this with a CASE statement instead of replacing the NULL value first:

CASE
    WHEN x2 IS NULL THEN x1
    ELSE x1 + (x1 * x2)
END

Q: Spinning thread takes 20,000 CPU cycles to see atomic write on Xeon CPU A:

Two things inflate a figure like the 20000 cycles reported here, and both are worth ruling out before coherence traffic is blamed.

The first cause that inflates the figure is the resolution of the observing loop: PAUSE costs about 10 cycles before Skylake and as many as 140 after it, so a loop that pauses between reads can only notice a change at that granularity: latency figures.

The second cause comes from the shape of the loop itself ;-) Reading with a plain load (without a lock), and attempting the atomic operation (with a LOCK prefix or that with implicit lock such as XCHG) only once the load looks promising, keeps the waiting core from issuing locked read-modify-writes against the line the writer needs exclusively. That load-then-attempt structure is the test-test-and-set shape the Intel optimisation manual recommends, and my own FastMM4-AVX, forked from FastMM4 by Pierre le Riche, spins that way for 5000 iterations before yielding.

As it stands the number measures the obsevring loop at least as much as it measures the hardware. Three details would decide between them: (1) the loop itself, which shows how coarsely it samples and whether it isseus locked operations while waiting; (2) the thread pinning, since two hyperthreads of one core and two separate sockets differ by an order of magnitude; (3) and the C-state configuration, since waking a core out of a deep sleep state costs microseconds that owe nothing to cache coherence. A genuine cross-socket (cross-NUMA node) transfer is a real cost, it is a different quantity from how long a loop took to notice one.

So I recommend you, as my reply, to make a real test as I suggested :-)

Q: Does Oracle Blockchain Platform support SmartBFT in Hyperledger Fabric 3.x? A:

As far as I know, Oracle Blockchain Platform doesn’t expose SmartBFT as a configurable ordering option. Fabric 3.x supporting BFT upstream, doesn’t mean OBP supports it too. You might check the specific OBP version before planning a 7-orderer setup.

Q: Why is xchg instruction with memory operand always atomic? A:

The atomicity is in the definition rather than in the prefix. With a memory operand, the processor applies its locking protocol for the whole exchange whether or not lock is written, so a bare xchg is already an atomic swap because for the xchg, the lock prefix is implicit, whereus for the other instructions it has to be explicit.

This atomcity costs what any locked read-modify-write costs. On Haswell and Kaby Lake parts, xchg [m],r and lock add [m],r both measure about 17 cycles of latency, roughly five times an unlocked store: measured latencies.

My FastMM4-AVX fork of FastMM4 relies on both halves of that: it takes a lock with a bare xchg and releases it with a plain mov, because only the acquire needs the exchange to be atomic. The locked form buys no faster propagation for that price: nothing pushes a cache line to another core, so a spinning core sees either release when its own load takes the line, on one socket or across several. The single difference is the store buffer, which a locked release drains and a plain store does not, so the plain store can land slightly later when the stores of the critical section are still queued ahead of it. That window is bounded by the buffer, while the lock prefix is paid in full on every unlock, upwards of a hundred clock cycles by Agner Fog's measurements, and the buffer behaiviour is the one described by x86-TSO. The x86 ordering rules make the plain store safe, which is why the Linux kernel releases a spinlock the same way. So when the release doesn't have to be immedate, the cheaper non-locking release is what I like ;-)
